text:
Based on this NSA documentation [1], they didn't actually synchronise the clocks with each other. They just tuned each machine's quartz oscillator with the nearest national time source. They were mostly dialling in the oscillator frequency here, not the exact time, so it didn't really matter they were synchronising to different national time standards.

Besides, even with the automated start system, the actual spin-up time of the turntables would have been a little chaotic. I suspect they were only aiming to get the four turntables within about 100ms of each other. The decrypted signal itself could then be used for the final fine-tuning of the timings (which also included adjusting for any speed-of-light delays)

If you weren't within 20ms, the operator would only hear noise (like a radio). Once they were within ~20ms, the operator would start hearing silence and would tune the phase until all noise went away.

You don't really need exact synchronisation because like a radio, the operator could just scrub the tuning to find the silence.

The synchronised clocks meant that once the operators had locked on, it would stay locked for a long time.

As mentioned, that had a tough sync problem. SIGSALY changed its key every 50ms. The mechanical synching of two turntables within that range was possible. That worked because the audio was being compressed pretty hard before encryption.
Delilah, which works by using a modular analog adder to add signal and key noise, would need a new analog key value for every audio sample. Probably 3KHz or so, or about 300usec. That's beyond the precision of sync which can be achieved reliably by mechanical means.

A little bit of analog buffer would help. 
It wouldn't be a problem for transistor era electronics. You need something like an analog shift register (see "bucket-brigade device"[1]) Those were not developed until the 1970s, and, for a while, appeared in guitar pedals, reverbs, and other simple audio processing devices. Fun retro electronics project for someone.

> The context gets added back to the latent vectors (which are the Q,K inputs) after every transformer layer, so they are "at least 50% words".

Not in a modern decoder-only transformer it doesn't. The tokens are turned into embeddings which are fed into the residual layer at the front. From then on it's latents all the way down.

Each layer does a feed forward update of the state, like the euler step in ODE solver-- but what they're operating on is the evolving hidden state and not the tokens/embeddings. So there isn't any sense in which the representations must remain 'words'.

(Okay fine Qwen3.8-flash-next injects an ngram embedding at layer 2 too-- but that's it).
